summary: To ensure baseline interoperability, WebRTC endpoints must support a minimum set of audio codecs. This informational RFC gives guidelines on other suitable codecs worth offering, to avoid transcoding when setting up sessions.

plainLanguage.summary: Besides the required languages, it is good to also know a few more, so two callers can talk without a translator.

questions: how to avoid transcoding in webrtc
subtitle: Guidelines for additional audio codecs to avoid transcoding between WebRTC and legacy networks.

tldr.problem: WebRTC endpoints use Opus for audio, but legacy networks like mobile and DECT systems use different codecs. Without support for these codecs, calls between WebRTC and legacy devices require transcoding, which degrades quality and adds cost.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC recommends three additional audio codecs for WebRTC endpoints: AMR-WB (wideband audio for 3GPP mobile), AMR (narrowband audio for older mobile), and G.722 (wideband audio for DECT phones and IMS). Supporting these allows direct, transcoding-free calls.
tldr.outcome: The recommended codecs enable WebRTC endpoints to interoperate seamlessly with existing mobile and VoIP infrastructure without quality loss or extra latency from transcoding.

today: RFC 7875 is an Informational RFC published in May 2016 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the definitive guidance for WebRTC endpoints seeking interoperability with legacy voice networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: WebRTC endpoints must implement Opus as a mandatory codec to ensure baseline interoperability between WebRTC applications. However, Opus is not widely supported in existing telephone networks. Many WebRTC endpoints need to connect with mobile phones using 3GPP networks, DECT cordless phones, or VoIP services that do not support Opus. When a WebRTC endpoint calls a device that does not share a common codec, the call must be converted from one codec to another. This conversion process, called transcoding, introduces significant problems for call quality, latency, and network costs.
sections.plainLanguage: WebRTC apps use Opus, which regular phones do not understand. If you want to call someone on a regular phone, you need a translator, but translators are slow and make your voice sound worse.

sections.title: Why Transcoding Causes Problems
sections.content:
Transcoding between different audio codecs has three main drawbacks. First, it degrades voice quality: converting audio from Opus to another codec and back results in a quality loss of about 0.2 to 0.3 MOS (Mean Opinion Score, a measure of perceived audio quality). If transcoding falls back to G.711, a much older narrowband codec used by traditional telephone networks, wideband quality is lost entirely, significantly reducing perceived call quality.

Second, transcoding adds latency because the process requires decompressing the entire audio stream, re-encoding it with a different codec, and resending it. This adds up to a full second of additional delay in some cases, far beyond what users find acceptable in a conversation. Third, transcoding costs money and computational resources. Network gateways that perform transcoding require codec implementations, licensing fees, testing, and deployment resources. Wideband-to-wideband transcoding requires even more CPU power than narrowband conversions.
sections.plainLanguage: Translators cost money, slow down the call, and sometimes lose parts of what you said. If the translator is bad, you might not understand each other well.

sections.title: Three Recommended Additional Codecs
sections.content:
AMR-WB (Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband) is the standard wideband codec for 3GPP mobile networks and is mandatory in any terminal that supports wideband voice over LTE (VoLTE). It is now the codec used by the vast majority of HD voice services on mobile phones. If WebRTC endpoints support AMR-WB, they can call any mobile 3GPP device without transcoding. Additionally, many WebRTC endpoints running on smartphones can reuse the AMR-WB codec already built into the phone hardware.

AMR (Adaptive Multi-Rate) is the narrowband codec used by 3GPP mobile networks and is still widely deployed in older mobile phones that do not yet support HD voice or wideband codecs. Although the number of narrowband-only devices is decreasing, supporting AMR ensures compatibility with legacy mobile handsets and allows these older devices to call WebRTC endpoints at acceptable quality.

G.722 is an ITU-T wideband codec approved in 1988 and is widely used in DECT cordless phones and broadband VoIP systems. It is the mandatory wideband codec for DECT CAT-iq terminals and has been approved by GSMA for fixed broadband HD voice. Supporting G.722 enables seamless calling between WebRTC endpoints and DECT phones or fixed VoIP systems without transcoding.
sections.plainLanguage: AMR-WB works with modern cellphones and gets good sound. AMR works with old cellphones. G.722 works with home phones and DECT cordless phones. Learning all three lets you call almost anyone.

sections.title: Implementation Guidelines
sections.content:
For AMR-WB, the RFC specifies that WebRTC endpoints should offer both AMR-WB and AMR, with AMR-WB listed as the preferred wideband codec. The endpoint must be able to operate with any subset of the nine AMR-WB codec modes and should offer at least one configuration matching the settings defined in 3GPP TS 26.114 for IMS compatibility. The bandwidth-efficient RTP payload format defined in RFC 4867 should be used.

For AMR, endpoints should similarly support both any subset of the eight AMR codec modes and follow the 3GPP TS 26.114 configuration for 4G/VoLTE systems. For G.722, the payload format is defined in RFC 3551. A notable quirk: although G.722 encodes at 16 kHz, the RTP clock rate is set to 8000 Hz for backward compatibility with an old definition in the RTP audio/video profile.
sections.plainLanguage: To support these codecs, you need to follow the rules in the 3GPP and ITU-T standards. Each codec has specific ways to encode and send audio that make sure all phones understand it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This RFC defers detailed security considerations to RFC 7874 (WebRTC Audio Codec and Processing Requirements) and to the specific standards for each recommended codec. Implementers should refer to the security sections of RFC 4867 (for AMR and AMR-WB payload formats) and RFC 3551 (for the RTP audio/video profile and G.722 handling). The security properties of these codecs are well-established by their existing deployments in 3GPP and DECT systems.
sections.plainLanguage: These codecs are used safely in mobile phones and home phones already, so the security work is done. Just follow the standards closely.
